sources.news_title: Trump Waives Russia Sanctions Before They Hit; GOP Balks
sources.text:
President Donald Trump signed an executive order late Friday waiving nearly every substantive sanction, tariff and trade restriction on Russia contained in a law he himself signed four weeks ago, halting the measures two days before they were due to take effect and setting off a rare wave of criticism from Republicans who had voted for the bill.
The order suspends the core provisions of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, the bipartisan package named for the late South Carolina senator who championed it for more than a year before his death in July. Trump told Congress in a one-line certification that the waiver was "in the national interests of the United States." The order offered no further explanation, and the White House had not elaborated by Saturday evening.
"I am hereby waiving the application of such sanctions, restrictions, and duties provided for in the Graham Act," the order reads, citing a clause in the statute that allows the president to set aside any sanctions provision aimed at foreign persons so long as he notifies Congress and submits a report explaining the basis for the decision.
The timing drew as much attention as the substance. The waiver came one week after the administration announced a deal under which Russia would ship 300,000 tons of diesel to the United States and world markets, a transaction that required a separate general license easing restrictions on Russian diesel exports through April 2027. It also came hours before Russia launched one of its largest aerial attacks of the autumn on Ukraine, and on the same weekend that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky was pleading with European leaders in Brussels for interceptors his air defenses no longer have.
Zelensky responded on Saturday morning with a statement that avoided Trump's name but left no doubt about its target.
"At a time when the Russians have carried out such a massive attack on our energy sector, a decision was unfortunately made in America to completely disregard the Lindsey Graham Act, which was supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end," he wrote on X. "This Act could have helped enormously — and still can! But it needs to actually work, and every voice in support of it matters."
He said the waiver was wrong, predicted it would not be the last, and posted photographs of himself with Graham, who had visited Kyiv repeatedly before his death. "Thank you for everything, Lindsey!" the caption read. In a separate post he was blunter: "Sanctions relief will continue. I think the diesel deal and the move regarding the Lindsey Graham Act are not the end of it. Unfortunately."
The Graham Act passed the House on Sept. 16 and was signed into law two days later, in a ceremony framed as a posthumous tribute to its namesake. Its central mechanism was a tariff of up to 500 percent on Russian goods and a secondary tariff of up to 100 percent on imports from countries that continued to buy large volumes of Russian oil and gas or that helped Moscow evade existing sanctions. A separate section codified and expanded earlier executive-branch sanctions on Russian financial institutions, state entities and energy projects, and authorized penalties on American investment in Russia.
The law's authors built in a waiver to give the president room to negotiate, but they paired it with reporting requirements intended to make any waiver politically costly. Friday's order satisfies the letter of that requirement with a single certification. It does not touch the sanctions that already exist under previous executive orders, which remain in force, and it does not affect the Iran-related provisions of the act.
What it does do is remove, before a single tariff was collected, the only new economic pressure on Russia that Congress has enacted since the war began. For the countries that buy the most Russian crude — China, India and Turkey among them — the secondary tariff was the provision that mattered, because it would have forced a choice between Russian barrels and the American market. That choice has now been deferred indefinitely.
Republican reaction on Saturday was sharper than the White House appears to have anticipated. Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina, who is retiring and has grown increasingly willing to break with the president, called the decision "beyond irresponsible." Sen. John Cornyn of Texas said Graham "would be appalled" and circulated a National Review editorial urging Congress to investigate the waiver. Rep. Don Bacon of Nebraska, a retired Air Force general and one of the House's most consistent supporters of Ukraine, added his own criticism on social media.
The defense came from the other end of the party. Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, one of seven House Republicans who voted against the bill, said he was "glad to see Trump has used the executive authority granted to him by Congress to waive almost all of the provisions of this stupid law that pertain to Russia."
Democrats were uniformly hostile, with several senators arguing that the waiver amounted to a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin at the moment his economy is under the most strain it has faced since 2022. Russia banned diesel exports earlier this month after Ukrainian drone strikes on refineries cut domestic supply, and its oil revenue has been squeezed by a combination of Western price caps and the Hormuz crisis that has scrambled global energy flows.
That crisis is the key to understanding the administration's calculus. Diesel prices in the United States have risen sharply since the Iran war closed the Strait of Hormuz to most commercial traffic in February, and the September consumer price index released this week showed inflation at 3.7 percent with fuel the largest contributor. With the midterm elections 17 days away, the White House has made lowering pump prices its overriding domestic objective, and it has pursued that objective through Moscow as readily as through Riyadh.
The diesel deal announced Oct. 9 was the first step. The administration has since signaled it is considering easing sanctions on shadow-fleet tankers carrying Russian products, and the Graham Act waiver removes the one measure that would have made those steps legally awkward. Had the 500 percent tariff taken effect on Sunday, Russian diesel entering American ports would have been subject to it; the waiver resolves that contradiction in Moscow's favor.
Kirill Dmitriev, the head of Russia's sovereign wealth fund and the Kremlin's main interlocutor with Trump's envoys, welcomed the order within hours. "The U.S.-Russia economic dialogue and peacemaking efforts will continue," he wrote, in language that implied the waiver was the product of that dialogue rather than a unilateral act. Trump himself, speaking to reporters last weekend, had suggested Ukraine should "get a new leader who can make a deal," adding that the war "should have never started" without mentioning that Russia started it.
The personal rupture between the two presidents has been widening for a month. Trump's demand on Oct. 11 for an "energy ceasefire" was followed within hours by a Russian strike on a Kharkiv power plant, and Ukraine's three-day pause in refinery strikes ended when Zelensky accused Washington of cutting intelligence sharing. In Brussels on Friday he warned that the diesel deal "could set a precedent for further sanctions relief" and told Piers Morgan earlier in the week that he felt "betrayed" by it. "Sanctions will be lifted after gas," he predicted — a forecast that proved accurate within 48 hours.
Russia's actions over the same weekend sharpened the contrast the waiver's critics were drawing. Ukraine's air force said Moscow fired more than 330 drones and missiles overnight into Saturday, of which 293 were suppressed or shot down. One person was killed and 19 wounded in the Kherson region, five were wounded in a strike on a residential district of Zaporizhzhia, and Zelensky said more than 15 power generation and transmission facilities were hit across the country.
Russia's Defense Ministry described the operation as a "massive strike" on metallurgical plants, a transformer factory and energy infrastructure in Kryvyi Rih, Zaporizhzhia and Zhytomyr. It said its forces also hit two cargo vessels in and near the port of Odesa that it claimed were carrying military and dual-use cargo, and later in the day reported further strikes on a vehicle-repair plant in Lutsk and a substation in the Ternopil region. The ArcelorMittal steelworks in Kryvyi Rih, Ukraine's largest, had already suspended operations in September after a series of ballistic-missile attacks; the company did not comment on Saturday's claims, which could not be independently verified.
Ukraine struck back at Moscow on the same night. Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said air defenses had intercepted 195 drones headed for the capital since midnight, one of the largest numbers reported in a single night, and Russian officials said drone attacks killed three people in border regions.
The exchange underscores why the Graham Act mattered to Kyiv beyond its direct economic effect. The law had been sold to Ukraine's European backers as evidence that the United States would use leverage on Moscow as well as on Kyiv. European governments had aligned their own 20th sanctions package with it, and the EU summit that Zelensky attended on Friday had been expected to discuss how to coordinate secondary measures against buyers of Russian crude. The waiver leaves that coordination without an American anchor.
It also exposes a tension inside the administration's Iran strategy. The Graham Act's Iran provisions remain in force, and the Treasury Department this week announced a new round of sanctions on Iran's shadow fleet and its financial networks. The United States is, in effect, tightening the energy noose on one adversary while loosening it on another, and the stated rationale for both is the same: oil prices. Analysts at the Atlantic Council and elsewhere noted that Russian crude freed from the threat of secondary tariffs will flow more readily to the same Asian refiners that Washington is pressing to shun Iranian barrels.
For Republicans facing voters in November, the waiver complicates a message the party had settled on: that Trump was tough on Putin, as proven by the sanctions bill he signed in Graham's name. Tillis's language — "beyond irresponsible" — is the kind usually reserved for the opposition, and Cornyn's invocation of Graham's memory suggests the senator's death has removed a restraint on how far his former colleagues will go in public.
The waiver is not permanent. The statute allows Congress to pass a joint resolution of disapproval, and the president must renew his certification periodically or allow the measures to take effect. Whether a Republican-controlled Congress would move against a Republican president on a foreign-policy question three weeks before an election is doubtful, and the calls for an investigation from National Review and Cornyn are, for now, calls.
In Moscow, the practical effect is immediate. Russian refiners that had been preparing for a potential loss of Indian and Chinese customers now have no reason to discount their crude further, and the Kremlin can present the waiver domestically as proof that its wartime economy has outlasted Western resolve. The Russian Finance Ministry had already been counting on the diesel deal to ease a budget shortfall caused by lower export volumes; the waiver removes a second source of uncertainty.
In Kyiv, the effect is harder to measure but no less real. Ukraine has lost, in the space of one week, a diesel-market advantage it had earned through refinery strikes, an American intelligence channel it says has been cut, and the prospect of secondary sanctions it had spent a year lobbying for. Its air force has run short of Patriot interceptors, as Zelensky told European leaders on Friday, and the strikes on its power grid are arriving at the rate of one major attack every two or three days as winter approaches.
The question that will follow the president into the final stretch of the campaign is the one Zelensky posed obliquely on Saturday: whether the waiver is the end of the administration's sanctions relief for Russia or the beginning. Trump has said repeatedly that the Iran war will end "right after the midterms" and that oil prices will "drop like a rock" when it does. If that forecast holds, the economic case for sparing Russia disappears in November. If it does not, the pressure to find cheaper fuel wherever it can be found will only grow — and Moscow, having tested the administration's priorities twice in one week, now knows which way it leans.
The sanctions the order waived were scheduled to take effect on Sunday.

sources.news_title: Trump executive order blocks U.S. sanctions on Russia
What Trump’s Waiver of New Russia Sanctions Means for Ukraine
sources.text:
President Donald Trump signed an executive order Friday that waives many of the sanctions in the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which Congress passed in the late senator’s name last month. The waiver, coming a week after Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia, also underscores fraying relations between the U.S. and Ukraine.
The law, which was set to take effect Oct. 18, called for sanctions targeting Russian officials, financial institutions, and other entities, alongside tariffs of up to 100% on goods imported into the U.S. from major buyers of Russian crude oil or natural gas. Those measures were intended to restrict the financial resources supporting Russia’s war against Ukraine.
Read More: Lawmakers Argue Trump's Russia Diesel Deal 'Violates' the Law. Here's What Legal Experts Say
The U.K.’s Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office estimated in June 2025 that international sanctions had deprived the Russian state of at least $450 billion in war funds since February 2022, including through lost oil tax revenues and immobilized central-bank reserves.
While Trump’s waiver leaves existing sanctions in place, it blocks the additional pressure the new measures were intended to exert.
Trump has also pushed Ukraine to scale back its own campaign against Russia’s energy sector, repeatedly urging Kyiv to halt strikes on Russian fuel infrastructure and suggesting that those attacks are driving up U.S. fuel prices. But Ukrainian strikes are only one factor affecting fuel prices; disruptions linked to the war with Iran are largely responsible for constraining global supplies, while reduced Russian refinery activity has added pressure to diesel markets.
On Oct. 11, Trump claimed that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an “energy ceasefire.” But Ukrainian officials reported Russian strikes on energy infrastructure hours after his announcement, and Zelensky said the purported agreement was news to him.
That same day, Trump called for Ukraine to replace President Volodymyr Zelensky. Withdrawing sanctions within a week of those statements, and thereby improving Russia’s financial position, points to an increasingly uneven display of support from the U.S.
Jeff Colgan, a professor of political science at Brown University, tells TIME that the decision is basically “is like trading [Ukrainian] democracy for diesel.”
A diesel deal with Russia, announced Oct. 9, is one of the many recent actions Trump has taken in an effort to reduce fuel prices for Americans ahead of midterm elections on Nov. 3. The deal came with an easing of sanctions as the Treasury Department issued a temporary license authorizing transactions involving Russian diesel, including imports into the U.S., through April 7, 2027.
In his announcement of the deal on Truth Social, Trump said that Russia had agreed to supply global markets with more than 4.8 million tons of diesel, claiming that it would bring diesel prices down “IN RECORD NUMBERS.”
But experts question whether the deal would actually have any material impact on the price of fuel for American consumers.
“There could be a modest short-term effect on wholesale prices, but only a small and delayed benefit, if any, would reach consumers at the pump,” says Tatiana Mitrova, a fellow at Columbia University's Center on Global Energy Policy.
The waiver signed Friday, in comparison, could potentially prevent additional disruption to the global energy market. It allows Russian oil to continue flowing to importers like China and India, preventing further market volatility.
“The broader sanctions waiver may prevent additional market disruptions, but it does not itself create new supply,” Mitrova says. “The potential economic benefit to American consumers looks rather modest compared with the geopolitical cost of weakening sanctions pressure.”
Reducing that pressure—which has widely been interpreted as a component of the diesel deal, though it has not been explicitly identified as such—likely benefits Russia more than the monetary value of the diesel deal itself, Mitrova points out.
“The much bigger financial benefit for Moscow is avoiding additional sanctions that could have undermined its much larger crude oil export revenues,” she says.
And while Trump has touted the benefits of the deal, Colgan questions whether they will be tangible to any country other than Russia itself.
“Easing the sanctions probably won't move global prices very much (big market), but could mean substantial extra revenue for Russia,” he says.
But the potential consequences extend beyond Russia’s balance sheet. The waiver also raises questions about Washington’s commitment to Ukraine as relations between the two countries deteriorate.
How might the sanctions waiver affect Ukraine?
Beyond its impact on global diesel prices, Trump’s sanctions waiver could deepen a growing rift between the U.S. and Ukraine—raising further questions about Washington’s support for Kyiv.
Konstantin Sonin, a Russian economist and a professor at the University of Chicago Harris School of Public Policy, reads the move as a symbolic gesture of support for Russian President Vladimir Putin. He suggests that it could send a message to U.S. allies that extends beyond economic considerations.
“I think this will be read by Ukraine and Ukraine leadership—and European leadership—as another step in the United States withdrawing from being an active European player,” he tells TIME.
In addition to bolstering Russia’s finances and giving it latitude in its invasion of Ukraine, Sonin says that the waiver of additional sanctions could also “boost morale” for Putin.
“It’s another bit of signaling that the United States is not as supportive of Ukraine as they were historically,” he adds. “You still cannot say that the United States is on Putin's side, but it is another bit of diminishing support for Ukraine.”
Mitrova agrees that the biggest benefit to Russia might be more strategic than financial.
“For Putin, the most valuable outcome may not be additional diesel revenues but the perception that Washington is increasingly prioritizing domestic energy prices over sustained pressure on Russia,” she says. “That could reinforce the Kremlin’s belief that it can outlast Western support rather than make meaningful concessions.”
Zelensky criticized the decision to block the new sanctions.

Mitrova argues that in easing sanctions, the U.S. also compromises its position with European leadership that has continued to align closely with Zelensky and Ukraine.
“Europe is still tightening sanctions against Russia, while Washington is now moving in the opposite direction,” she says. “By suspending sanctions that were designed to discourage major countries from buying Russian energy, Washington risks undermining a central pillar of the Western strategy toward Russia.”
Why Republicans and Democrats are criticizing the waiver
Trump’s waiver earned a flood of criticism from both sides of the aisle, particularly since it undermined a widely supported act of Congress. The Sanctioning Russia Act of 2026 cleared Congress on Sept. 16 with overwhelming bipartisan support: a vote of 86-11 in the Senate and a vote of 262-159 in the House.
North Carolina Republican Sen. Thom Tillis, who is leaving office in January, called the decision “beyond irresponsible” on Saturday.

Texas Republican Sen. John Cornyn reacted by saying “Lindsey would be appalled,” referencing the late Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham—a staunch Ukraine supporter after whom the sanctions act was named. Graham had spent over a year petitioning for the move before his death on July 11.
Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat, said in a statement that Trump was “enabling Vladimir Putin to continue his war of aggression.”
Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer released a statement Saturday saying that “by giving the Russian economy life support, Trump’s deal with the devil keeps getting dirtier.”
Trump was able to waive the sanctions through a safety valve provision embedded in the legislation. The law allowed Trump to waive its sanctions and tariffs after submitting a written certification to Congress that doing so was in the national interest, along with a report explaining that determination. In Friday’s order, Trump said he had submitted both.
“I am hereby waiving the application of such sanctions, restrictions, and duties provided for in the Graham Act,” Trump wrote in the order. “I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver at this time is in the national interests of the United States.”
A White House spokesperson tells TIME that enforcing the sanctions would impede U.S. efforts to negotiate peace, but did not elaborate.
"Enforcing the sanctions provisions now would impede ongoing U.S. efforts to negotiate a durable and comprehensive peace agreement between Ukraine and Russia," the spokesperson says. "The President retains the ability to exercise these authorities at any time if he determines that doing so would advance national interests.”
Darline Graham, the late senator’s sister who was appointed to fill his seat in South Carolina and is running for election this November to keep it, said at a campaign stop on Saturday that the decision was Trump’s to make; however, she voiced disapproval, saying that she would prefer to “keep the pressure on Russia.”
“I don’t trust Putin and I don’t trust Russia,” she said.

KYIV, Ukraine — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy urged supporters Saturday to speak out in favor of new U.S. sanctions against Russia, hours after President Donald Trump signed an executive order putting the sweeping restrictions on hold.
The White House decision has heightened fears that Ukraine could be left exposed to Moscow’s escalating attacks as winter approaches.
Overnight Russian attacks killed at least four people, including an ambulance driver, and wounded dozens, officials said. Ukrainian drones killed a woman in a Russian border region and disrupted flights at Moscow’s airports, according to Russian authorities.
In a social media statement, Zelenskyy called Trump’s decision unfortunate but avoided directly criticizing the U.S. leader despite deepening tensions between Ukraine and Washington in recent days.
“A decision was unfortunately made in America to completely disregard the Lindsey Graham Act, which was supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end,” Zelenskyy wrote. “This Act could have helped enormously – and still can! But it needs to actually work, and every voice in support of it matters.”
He separately thanked Democrats and Republicans who supported the legislation, saying that blocking it would encourage Russia to continue killing and that limiting Ukraine’s ability to retaliate would not bring peace.
“Nevertheless, we very much hope — and I personally hope — that the president of the United States of America will do everything possible to make (Russian President Vladimir) Putin stop the killing, stop the attacks on our energy infrastructure, and end this war,” he said.
Asked about contacts with Washington, Zelenskyy said Ukraine’s lead negotiator, Rustem Umerov, had met Friday with U.S. presidential envoy Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law.
Zelenskyy said the U.S. was working to arrange a three-way meeting involving him, Trump and Putin, potentially in the Middle East, Europe or the United States.
Critics say Trump's decision helps Putin
Named after late South Carolina Sen. Lindsey Graham, the legislation had sought to clamp down more quickly on the flow of financial resources fueling Russia's 4 1/2-year-old war against Ukraine. The bill had sought to sanction Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers that keeps Russian energy moving.
Trump personally signed the legislation just last month and his move came just two days before a deadline set in the law itself for its implementation. Trump told Congress that the pause was in the national interest but gave no further details.
Sen. Richard Blumenthal, who co-drafted the bill, criticized Trump's move, saying the president was turning his back on “the majority of Americans, their representatives in both houses of Congress, and our European allies.”
“These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, and everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin,” Blumenthal said.
Trump’s unexpected decision comes a week after he had agreed to purchase diesel from Russia to try to bring down global energy prices, despite that potentially hurting Ukraine. Republicans and Democrats alike say the purchase will help Russia execute its war against Ukraine — without making a difference to global fuel prices, which are elevated mostly due to Trump’s war on Iran.
Starlink restrictions were planned, Zelenskyy says
Zelenskyy said that Kyiv was investigating sudden speed restrictions on Ukraine’s use of Starshield, the military-grade version of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite internet service, which is the backbone of Ukraine’s drone operations and communication.
The restrictions, imposed without warning early Thursday, cut the internet data connection when a communication terminal moves faster than 160 kph (100 mph). The cap forced Ukrainian drones to fly slower than usual, making it easier for Russian weapons to target or evade them.
Zelenskyy said that there were no similar restrictions in European Union countries and that they apply only to Ukraine. “In other words, this is a planned operation,” he said.
It was unclear who was responsible. SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk said this week that the U.S. government owns and controls the system, with decisions about its use resting with the U.S. military and, ultimately, the president. The Pentagon has not answered questions from The Associated Press about the restrictions.
Trump told reporters Friday that he did not order restrictions on the system. He also doubted that the disruption came from Musk.
“Well, I don’t know if it was anybody, but it wasn’t me, and I don’t think it was Elon,” Trump said. “And from what I understand, it’s the same as it’s always been.”
Kyiv reports a ‘massive’ energy strike
Moscow carried out a massive strike on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, targeting more than 15 sites across the country, Zelenskyy said.
“The sheer scale and unrelenting pace of Russia’s strikes, specifically against our energy sector, are unfortunately having severe consequences,” he said.
Ukraine’s air force said it intercepted all four of Russia's cruise missiles and most of the 332 attack drones it fired overnight.
Russia’s heavy bombardment of the power grid ahead of winter has been an annual feature of the war, aimed at wearing down Ukraine’s appetite for the fight by denying civilians heat and running water. Ukrainian officials have warned that Russia is stockpiling ballistic missiles for more attacks in the coming months.
Russian attacks killed three people in the Ukrainian city of Sloviansk, Vadym Liakh, head of the city military administration, said Saturday. A Russian strike also killed an ambulance driver in Ukraine’s Kherson region, head of the local military administration Yaroslav Shanko said. The strike, which used guided bombs, wounded at least 33 others, he said.
Ukrainian drones disrupt Moscow airports
A Russian woman was killed in a Ukrainian drone attack in the Russian border region of Belgorod, local officials said.
Russia’s Ministry of Defense said Saturday that its forces shot down 610 Ukrainian drones overnight over 15 Russian regions, as well as the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black Sea.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said that more than 100 drones were shot down en route to the capital. More than 350 flights were canceled or delayed at Moscow airports, local media reported, as planes were grounded in response to incoming drones.
The Kremlin announced Saturday that Putin approved a government program to help restore trade and logistics facilities damaged in drone attacks
Romania downs 2 drones over Black Sea
Romania’s Ministry of National Defense said Saturday that its pilots had shot down two drones over the country’s territorial waters in the Black Sea.
Two F-16s were scrambled at 5:43 p.m. local time after radar systems “detected a group of aerial targets moving southwest, approximately 120 kilometers east of Snake Island,” the ministry said.
The drones entered the NATO member’s airspace around 6 p.m. and were shot down minutes later.
“Both aerial targets were identified as drones and were shot down over Romania’s territorial waters,” the ministry said.
The incident follows a spate of drone attacks on at least seven cargo vessels off the Black Sea coasts of NATO members Romania and Bulgaria in October.
Scores of drones have crossed into Romanian airspace over the past two years, with officials attributing many of the incursions to Russia. Romania first shot down drones this year, marking its first such action since Moscow invaded neighboring Ukraine.
___
Davies reported from Manchester, England. Stephen McGrath contributed from Leamington Spa, England.

President Donald Trump has used a national-interest waiver to pause the sweeping Russia sanctions Congress passed with overwhelming bipartisan support — and some of the sharpest criticism is coming from inside his own party.
The move does not repeal the new law. It does something more immediate: it suspends the law’s major economic penalties while the White House decides what comes next.
That distinction matters. So does the timing.
The order arrived just two days before the sanctions were due to take effect, as Russia continued pounding Ukraine’s energy system and the administration pursued a separate diplomatic and commercial track with Moscow.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia had just carried out one of its largest attacks on Ukraine’s energy sector, hitting more than 15 critical power-generation and transmission facilities across multiple regions. Repair crews were still working as the sanctions debate broke open in Washington.
Yesterday, the Russians carried out one of their largest attacks on Ukraine’s energy sector – more than 15 critical power generation and transmission facilities were targeted across different regions of Ukraine. Restoration work is ongoing, with all necessary services and all… pic.twitter.com/nEhkkjxwXa
— Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) October 17, 2026
The contrast is stark: the administration is withholding new economic pressure at the same moment Kyiv says Moscow is escalating attacks on the civilian power grid. That makes the waiver a test of whether promised leverage can alter Russian behavior before the penalties ever bite.
The legal mechanism is laid out in the administration’s own order, and it is broader than a routine enforcement delay. The decision reaches the central penalties Congress designed to squeeze both Moscow and the foreign buyers keeping its energy trade alive.
The White House executive order begins by implementing the new Russia and Iran sanctions law, which President Trump signed on September 18. It establishes a 500 percent duty on Russian goods and a 100 percent duty on goods from countries found to be buying or facilitating Russian oil and uranium.
The order also targets Russian officials, financial institutions, energy entities and vessels operating in Moscow’s so-called shadow fleet. Section 4 then invokes the statute’s national-interest authority and waives those duties, sanctions and restrictions until the president and senior officials determine that further action is warranted.
In plain English: the enforcement machinery is now built, but the president has pulled the emergency brake before it starts moving.
That gives Trump leverage. The administration can argue that it now holds a congressionally authorized economic hammer over Russia, China, India and any other country facilitating Moscow’s energy trade — without swinging it immediately.
It also gives critics an obvious counterargument: a hammer that never falls may not be leverage at all.
Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina did not bother with diplomatic language. He called the decision “beyond irresponsible” and stressed that the sanctions law passed the Senate 86-11.
Beyond irresponsible. What part of enforcing a law passed 86-11 by the Senate does the President and his advisors not understand? It’s unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine and butchers innocent civilians every…
— Senator Thom Tillis (@SenThomTillis) October 17, 2026
The dispute is especially combustible because the law bears the name of the late Senator Lindsey Graham, one of Trump’s closest allies and one of Washington’s most persistent advocates for crushing economic pressure on Moscow.
Senator John Cornyn of Texas made that point with one devastating line: “Lindsey would be appalled.”
Lindsey would be appalled: Trump Signs Order Exempting Russia From Sanctions Law https://t.co/9tF3CBc3pL
— Senator John Cornyn (@JohnCornyn) October 17, 2026
The Associated Press reports that the waiver landed shortly before the law’s implementation deadline, after Congress assembled a broad package aimed at Russian officials, banks, oil revenue and the fleet used to evade existing restrictions. The timing transformed what could have been a quiet administrative choice into an immediate confrontation with lawmakers who expected the penalties to take effect.
The report also points to a separate commercial agreement under which a U.S. company would provide diesel fuel to Russia. That deal helps explain why senators regard the waiver as a substantive policy turn instead of a technical pause.
Administration defenders describe the delay as part of a larger attempt to preserve negotiating room with Moscow. Critics see economic relief being offered before Russia has made a meaningful concession on Ukraine, attacks on civilian infrastructure or any durable peace framework.
The disagreement therefore concerns more than the calendar. It asks whether holding sanctions in reserve increases American leverage or signals that the White House is reluctant to use the authority Congress supplied.
Axios adds that the backlash extends beyond Democrats, with Republican senators who backed the bill publicly challenging the White House. Kyiv, meanwhile, is warning that Russian attacks remain relentless while the new economic penalties sit idle.
The secondary sanctions were designed to pressure Moscow through the countries and companies that sustain its energy trade. Major buyers and intermediaries would have to decide whether access to Russian oil and uranium justified exposure to punishing U.S. tariffs.
Waiving those penalties removes the immediate deadline that was supposed to force that choice. It also gives foreign governments and markets time to test whether the threat is likely to become policy.
There is a strategic case for Trump’s approach.
Presidents traditionally want flexibility in foreign policy. The threat of sanctions can sometimes extract more than sanctions themselves, particularly if the target believes relief can be exchanged for a concrete concession.
Trump has always preferred direct negotiation, maximum uncertainty and deal-making over a timetable set by Congress.
The order also preserves the legal architecture. If negotiations fail, the administration can move quickly without returning to Congress for another vote.
But there is a serious risk in that strategy.
Russia has watched Western governments announce red lines, negotiate over deadlines and dilute enforcement for years. Every delay teaches the Kremlin something about American resolve.
If Moscow concludes that the sanctions will always be postponed in the name of keeping talks alive, the threat becomes theater.
Congress wrote the waiver into the law, so Trump is exercising authority lawmakers themselves provided. That legal point is clear.
The political question is harder: why pass a sanctions package by overwhelming margins, name it for one of the Senate’s loudest Russia hawks, and then suspend its central penalties before they ever take effect?
The White House now owns the answer.
If the pause produces measurable Russian concessions — a ceasefire, reduced attacks, prisoner releases, verifiable limits or a durable peace framework — Trump will argue that flexibility succeeded where reflexive punishment would have failed.
If Russia takes the relief, continues its offensive and offers nothing substantial in return, the senators warning about capitulation will look prescient.
The fight reaches far beyond another Washington argument over procedure. It is a live test of whether Trump’s deal-making style can restrain Vladimir Putin when a massive congressional sanctions weapon is already loaded and ready.
For now, the weapon remains on the table.
President Trump is the one who decided not to fire it.

President Trump Halts Sweeping Russia Sanctions, Citing America’s National Interest as Energy Prices Surge
President Trump has temporarily suspended a sweeping package of economic sanctions against Russia, invoking his authority under legislation passed by Congress to delay restrictions that could further disrupt global energy markets.
The president signed an executive order Friday waiving major provisions of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which he signed into law on September 18.
The legislation was designed to increase economic pressure on Moscow over its continued war against Ukraine, including imposing substantial tariffs on countries purchasing Russian oil and natural gas.
Trump informed Congress that implementing the restrictions at this time would not serve American interests.
“I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver at this time is in the national interests of the United States,” the president declared in his executive order.
The decision came just two days before several major sanctions provisions were scheduled to take effect on October 18.
Under the legislation, the United States could impose tariffs of up to 100% on goods imported from the five largest purchasers of Russian oil and natural gas.
The law also authorized a 500% tariff increase on Russian goods entering the United States, along with financial penalties targeting individuals and companies involved in supporting Moscow’s war effort.
Additional provisions were intended to restrict Russian banks, government officials and the network of oil tankers used to transport Russian petroleum around existing international sanctions.
Trump’s executive order preserves the legal framework for those measures while suspending their immediate enforcement.
The waiver will remain in effect until the president or senior administration officials determine that further action is appropriate.
The decision gives the White House flexibility to reconsider the restrictions without requiring Congress to repeal the legislation.
The president’s move comes as American consumers continue facing elevated gasoline and diesel prices amid international energy disruptions connected to the ongoing conflict involving Iran.
The administration has been searching for ways to stabilize fuel supplies and reduce economic pressure on American households.
Imposing substantial new tariffs on major Russian energy customers could complicate those efforts by disrupting international petroleum markets.
China and India, two of the world’s largest purchasers of Russian oil, have previously expressed concern about the potential consequences of the legislation.
Beijing has objected to American sanctions targeting commercial relationships between foreign countries, while New Delhi has warned that additional tariffs could damage economic relations with Washington.
The sanctions package had received strong bipartisan support in Congress following the death of Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham of South Carolina in July.
Graham had spent months advocating for tougher economic penalties against Russia, arguing that restricting Moscow’s energy revenue could force President Vladimir Putin to negotiate an end to the war.
The legislation was named in his honor and advanced with substantial support from Republicans and Democrats.
Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, who helped develop the measure, condemned Trump’s decision to suspend its enforcement.
Blumenthal accused the administration of weakening pressure on Putin and disregarding the intentions of lawmakers who approved the sanctions.
Democratic Rep. Don Beyer of Virginia also criticized the waiver, arguing that Congress should revisit the law to prevent the president from suspending its central provisions.
However, the waiver authority was explicitly included in the legislation approved by Congress.
Under Section 115, the president may suspend sanctions, restrictions and tariffs after submitting a written certification explaining why doing so serves the national interest.
Trump exercised that authority Friday, formally notifying lawmakers of his determination.
The White House did not immediately release a detailed public explanation of the economic and national security considerations behind the decision.
The suspension follows another major development in American relations with Moscow.
Last week, Trump announced an agreement under which Russia would supply substantial quantities of diesel fuel to international markets as part of an effort to reduce energy prices.
The arrangement reportedly included an initial shipment exceeding 300,000 tons, followed by additional supplies scheduled for November.
Trump presented the agreement as a practical response to rising fuel costs, although lawmakers from both parties questioned whether increased Russian energy sales could provide Moscow with additional revenue for its military operations.
The diesel arrangement also intensified disagreements between Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
Zelensky has repeatedly urged Washington to maintain strict economic pressure on Russia, arguing that reducing sanctions could encourage Moscow to prolong the conflict.
The Ukrainian president has also clashed with Trump over attacks on Russian oil refineries.
Trump recently criticized Ukraine’s decision to resume striking Russian energy facilities after an attempted agreement to halt attacks on energy infrastructure broke down.
The president argued that targeting refineries could contribute to higher international oil prices, creating economic consequences for countries far beyond the battlefield.
Zelensky has maintained that Ukraine must retain the ability to strike Russian energy infrastructure while Moscow continues attacking Ukrainian power stations and electrical facilities.
The disagreement has complicated American diplomatic efforts to secure a negotiated settlement.
Trump has repeatedly expressed frustration with the continued fighting and has called on both Russia and Ukraine to reach an agreement.
His administration has pursued direct engagement with Moscow while continuing discussions with Kyiv about possible conditions for ending the war.
The sanctions waiver represents another significant decision in that diplomatic approach.
Rather than immediately implementing additional economic penalties, Trump has retained the option to impose them later while avoiding new restrictions during a period of energy market instability.
The decision also arrives less than three weeks before the November 3 midterm elections.
Republicans are working to maintain control of Congress while facing questions about rising consumer costs, gasoline prices and the administration’s foreign policy decisions.
Higher energy prices have become a particularly sensitive economic issue as American families contend with increased transportation and household expenses.
The administration’s decision to delay the sanctions could reduce the risk of additional disruptions to fuel markets, although the actual impact on prices remains uncertain.
Meanwhile, Russia continues its military campaign in Ukraine, including attacks against energy infrastructure as winter approaches.
Ukrainian officials have warned that further strikes could leave civilians without reliable electricity and heating during colder weather.
The sanctions suspension does not end existing American restrictions against Russia. It delays enforcement of the additional measures authorized by the Graham Act.
Trump retains the ability to revisit the decision if diplomatic circumstances change or if the administration determines that stronger economic pressure is necessary.
For now, the president has chosen to preserve that leverage while prioritizing what he describes as the national interests of the United States.
The decision leaves Congress and the administration facing an important question: whether additional sanctions would bring Russia closer to negotiations or create further economic disruption without producing an end to the war.

— Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) October 17, 2026

“We said, ‘You can do whatever you want to Russia, [but] don’t hit the refineries because that’s a world problem that’s caused,’” Trump told reporters Oct. 10. “And he wants to make problems for the world. He wants to make problems for our farmer, our ranchers, with diesel fuel because Russia supplies a large portion of the diesel fuel throughout the world.”
“Personally, I would choose to put the pressure on Russia to end the war and get gas prices down,” Republican South Carolina Sen. Darline Graham, the sister of the bill’s namesake, told reporters Saturday. “Because I don’t trust Putin, and I don’t trust Russia.”
The U.S. Trade Representative’s office and Ukraine’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs did not immediately respond to the DCNF’s requests for comment.

Trump suspends Russia sanctions as deadly attacks plunge Ukraine into darkness
By Stefan Bos
U.S. President Donald Trump has suspended sweeping new sanctions against Russia, citing American national interests, as Russian missile and drone attacks killed at least eight people in Ukraine and left more than a million without electricity.
The decision has raised concerns over Washington’s approach to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and highlighted growing differences between the United States and the European Union over how to end the war.
Trump waived key Russia-related sanctions and tariffs just days before they were due to take effect under legislation he signed last month.
The measures included penalties against countries purchasing Russian oil and natural gas, intended to increase economic pressure on Moscow over its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Zelenskyy criticizes sanctions relief
The U.S. president cited American national interests amid rising energy prices. His decision followed a controversial agreement allowing more Russian diesel onto global markets, a move Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned would help finance Moscow’s military campaign.
Speaking about the impact on ordinary Ukrainians, Zelenskyy said the additional Russian diesel would do little to reduce fuel prices in the United States but would provide Russia with more money to continue its attacks.
He recalled how Ukrainian children had spent nearly five years growing up amid air raid warnings, seeking shelter underground or attending classes online.
“They didn’t have childhood because of one person, because Putin,” Zelenskyy said, referring to Russian President Vladimir Putin. “It’s a mistake. I’m sure this diesel will not help Americans but will help Putin,” he added.
Russian attacks kill civilians
His remarks came as Russian forces continued launching missile and drone strikes against Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure.
At least eight people were reportedly killed and 60 others injured in Friday’s attacks, while more than one million people lost electricity. Ukrainian authorities said repair crews subsequently restored power to more than a million people.
The destruction has renewed concerns about the humanitarian consequences of Russia’s campaign against Ukraine’s energy network, particularly for families, elderly residents and vulnerable communities facing the coming winter.
Against this backdrop, European Union leaders meeting at a summit in Brussels reaffirmed their support for Ukraine and expressed regret over Washington’s decision to ease restrictions on Russian diesel.
EU pledges military aid
EU leaders welcomed a new package of sanctions against Moscow and an agreement to release another 6.6 billion euros, approximately $7.5 billion, in military assistance through the European Peace Facility.
However, they stopped short of approving Zelenskyy’s request for an additional 70 billion euros in financial and military assistance for 2027, instead calling for further assessments of Ukraine’s funding needs.
The developments underscored growing differences between Washington and Brussels over the economic pressure needed to bring Moscow to the negotiating table.
As Russia’s full-scale invasion approaches its fifth anniversary in February, Ukraine faces mounting civilian casualties, widespread infrastructure damage and uncertainty over the global support needed to sustain its defense and secure a lasting peace.

sources.news_title: Trump’s decision to waive Russian sanctions outrages Congress - The Boston Globe
sources.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump’s abrupt decision to waive sanctions on Russia days before they were to take effect drew outrage Saturday from members of Congress, which had overwhelmingly passed the legislation in a bipartisan display of American support for Ukraine in the war with Russia.
Lawmakers from both parties blasted the executive order late Friday, the latest in a series of steps that the Republican president has taken drawing the United States closer to Russia’s Vladimir Putin. Trump recently announced a diesel deal with Putin to import Russian energy in a long-shot effort to curb high gas prices in the U.S. that are roiling the midterm elections on Nov. 3.
“Beyond irresponsible,” said Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., on social media, hours after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy expressed hope that the sanctions that were supposed to take effect Sunday targeting Russian’s economy could be revived.
“What part of enforcing a law passed 86-11 by the Senate does the President and his advisers not understand?” Tillis said. “It’s unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine.”
Tillis said that if Trump wants to actually bring down energy prices, he should resolve the Iran war, which is largely blamed for the spike at the pump, and “not by doing a solid for Vladimir Putin.”
Republican Sen. John Cornyn of Texas said “Lindsey would be appalled,” referring to the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., who worked endlessly on the bill before he died this summer. The bill is known as the Lindsey Graham Russian Sanctions Act.
Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., said Trump is “thumbing his nose” at Congress and “enabling Vladimir Putin to continue his war of aggression.” She urged her colleagues to take action to reverse course.
Trump’s actions come as Ukraine is bracing for a stark winter confronting Russia’s ongoing attacks on its energy infrastructure to heat homes and keep the lights on. Zelenskyy, who has endured a rocky relationship with Trump but stayed close to the U.S. lawmakers, urged supporters to speak out on behalf of the sanctions.
The next steps are highly uncertain with the House and Senate are on recess until after Election Day. Trump said he was waiving the sanctions indefinitely, citing national security concerns. It is unlikely Congress would be in a position to take any action to challenge Trump’s moves until lawmakers return to Washington.
Skeptics in Congress warned Trump would not follow the law
It took almost a year for Graham to persuade Trump to agree to the Russian sanctions package. It was designed to impose steep tariffs on countries that import large amounts of Russian oil and energy products and was promoted as way to halt the flow of funds fueling Putin’s four-year war against Ukraine.
But even as Zelenskyy had watched from the visitor gallery as the Senate advanced the package after Graham’s death, skeptics in Congress warned Trump would be unlikely to follow the bill once he had signed it into law a month ago.
Last week, a bipartisan group of senators urged the Trump administration to more quickly clamp down on Russia, particularly the “shadow fleet” of tankers that Moscow is using to transport oil and bypass America’s sanctions. The senators noted that the bulk of the new law’s provisions were to be effective Sunday.
Instead, Trump soon announced the diesel deal with Putin, saying that Russia had agreed to supply tons of fuel to the U.S., where gas prices have skyrocketed in some areas and voters saying affordability issues are a top concern.
Outraged lawmakers have pledged to stop the Trump-Putin deal.
New York Rep. Gregory Meeks, the ranking Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee who had led opposition to the Graham bill — warning that Trump would flout the law — introduced legislation Friday that would block Trump’s diesel deal with Putin. “At a time when the United States should be increasing pressure on the Kremlin, Donald Trump is cozying up to Putin and striking self-enriching deals instead of standing with Ukraine,” Meeks said in a statement.
He called the deal “corrupt” and said it “goes against everything the United States stands for.”
Associated Press writers Kevin Freking and Mary Clare Jalonick contributed to this report.

Trump waves Russia sanctions passed by Congress amid deepening row with Ukraine
Donald Trump has put on hold a sweeping new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy, telling Congress the pause on the legislation passed by both chambers was in the national interest, the Guardian reported.
In an executive order on Friday, the president said he was waiving many sanctions, restrictions and duties on Russia, in a move that comes as he has been publicly criticizing Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, including suggesting that Ukraine needs a new leader.
The move was greeted by Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev, who wrote on social media: “The Trump administration’s suspension of the Graham Act is an important and truly historic moment.”
Trump signed the legislation last month, after Congress passed the measure in an act of rare bipartisan agreement. It sought to clamp down more quickly on the flow of financial resources fueling Russia’s war in Ukraine.
The legislation – whose primary backer in Congress was the late senator Lindsey Graham – sanctions Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers that keeps Russian energy moving and was due to be implemented in two days.
It also directs Trump to impose up to 100% tariffs on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.
Friday’s announcement comes a week after Trump said the U.S. had agreed to purchase diesel from Russia to try to bring down global energy prices, upending years of U.S. and Western pressure on the Kremlin to end its war against Ukraine.
Trump said last week that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1m tons “immediately thereafter”. Russia would deliver an additional 3m tons “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote.
Under the legislation he signed into law, Trump had until October 18 to impose the sanctions and tariffs on Russian energy, or waive them. The administration had not told lawmakers whether it would impose the sanctions or issue a waiver.
Facing midterm elections on November 3, Trump has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for pushing up energy prices that could cost his Republican party its thin majorities in the US Senate and House of Representatives.

Trump Pauses Major Russia Sanctions and Tariffs Under New Law, Citing National Interest
WASHINGTON — As reported by Axios, President Trump has issued an executive order putting a sweeping new package of sanctions and tariffs targeting Russia on hold. The move comes just days before the measures were set to take effect under a bipartisan law passed by Congress.
According to Axios, the executive order signed late Friday halts restrictions that were mandated under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026. The legislation—named after the late South Carolina Republican senator who was a vocal champion of Ukraine—had successfully cleared majorities in both the House and Senate.
A Pivot on Russian Energy and Trade
The stalled legislation aimed to clamp down aggressively on the Russian economy by slapping heavy tariffs on imports from major buyers of Russian crude oil and natural gas, as well as countries aiding Moscow in circumventing existing sanctions.
However, as Axios detailed, the Trump administration has opted for a strategic waiver, arguing that pausing the sanctions serves the national interest. This decision coincides with a broader diplomatic and economic recalibration by the White House, which Axios noted has featured discussions and concessions involving Russian energy supplies, including an easing of restrictions on Russian diesel.
Supporters of the administration’s decision maintain that flexibility is vital to cooling domestic energy and fuel costs, and keeping a pathway open for negotiations aimed at ending the protracted conflict.
Pushback From Critics
The decision to waive the congressional mandates has drawn swift backlash from critics and congressional opponents. Lawmakers who backed the Graham Act argue that easing pressure on Moscow undermines Western leverage against the Kremlin at a critical juncture in the war.
With midterms approaching and foreign policy debates intensifying in Washington, Axios highlighted that the white-hot clash over how to handle trade, energy, and economic warfare against Russia remains a central flashpoint between the White House and Capitol Hill.

Congress passed the Russia sanctions bill named for Lindsey Graham with bipartisan support. Trump just put it on hold a month after signing it
sources.text:
President Donald Trump on Friday signed an executive order that puts on hold a sweeping new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy, telling Congress the pause was in the national interest.
Trump personally signed the legislation just last month and his move came just two days before a deadline set in the law itself for its implementation. It drew shift condemnation from congressional Democrats.
Named after late South Carolina Sen. Lindsey Graham, the legislation had sought to clamp down more quickly on the flow of financial resources fueling the war against Ukraine.
Trump’s unexpected decision comes a week after he stunningly said the U.S. had agreed to purchase diesel from Russia to try to bring down global energy prices, despite that potentially hurting Ukraine in its war with Russia.
An AP-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll published Oct. 1 found that Americans disapprove of the president’s handling of the Iran war and blame him for higher prices. Trump’s approval ratings have sunk to near-historic lows and pressure is mounting as Republicans try to hold control of both chambers of Congress after midterm elections on Nov. 3.
Sanctions were seen as part of Graham’s legacy
Graham, a close ally and friend of the president, had just returned from Ukraine when he unexpectedly died in July. He had advocated for stricter U.S. sanctions against Russia as a way of pressuring it to end its war in Ukraine.
His colleagues in Congress responded with bipartisan support after his death and Trump attached his signature to the legislation — then changed his mind Friday.
The package had been meant to starve Russian President Vladimir Putin of the resources Moscow needs to continue its war in Ukraine after invading its neighbor more than four years ago. The bill, also drafted by Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., had sought to sanction Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers that keeps Russian energy moving.
It also directed Trump to impose up to 100% tariffs on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.
Blumenthal said in a statement that Trump was turning his back on “the majority of Americans, their representatives in both houses of Congress, and our European allies.”
“These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, and everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin,” Blumenthal said.
Democratic Virginia Rep. Don Beyer noted on social media shortly after the announcement of the sanctions being suspended that he and others had “warned” Trump might make such a move. The veteran congressman, who spoke out against the bill as it was debated, called on Congress to “fix this flawed law to stop Trump from capitulating to Putin and ensure that it truly supports Ukraine.”
The White House did not immediately explain how pausing the sanctions was in the national interest. The decision was posted on the White House website late in the evening, and the notification noted that the report explaining the decision had been submitted to Congress.
Still, it comes as Trump has increasingly lashed out at Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, blaming him for failing to make a deal with Putin to end the fighting.
The Trump administration, meanwhile, had remained mostly quiet since the passage of the bill with large majorities in the House and Senate following Graham’s sudden death — with lawmakers urged ahead by Zelenskyy.
Trump’s action follows announced diesel deal with Putin
Under last week’s agreement, Trump said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.”

- —What is happening President Donald Trump signed an executive order on 16 October 2026 that activated but immediately waived 500% duties on Russian goods and 100% duties on major Russian energy buyers under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026.

- —What to watch The waiver has no fixed expiration date, but a separate temporary easing of sanctions on Russian diesel exports runs through April 2027, and any presidential or State Department determination could reactivate the duties with little notice.

The russia sanctions waiver signed by President Donald Trump on 16 October 2026 suspends, but does not eliminate, 500% duties on Russian goods and 100% tariffs on major buyers of Russian energy. For US firms and Latin American importers, the decision creates a period of commercial relief that could end with a single executive determination.
Brazil is a major agricultural economy and a major importer of fertiliser, including Russian fertiliser, while Mexico, Argentina, Chile, Colombia and Peru have varying exposure to Russian petroleum products. This analysis explains what the waiver means for those trade relationships and for American companies, drawing on the USA & Canada Intelligence Brief published on 17 October 2026.
What the Order Says and Why It Was Waived
The executive order implements the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which President Trump signed on 18 September 2026. The law authorizes a duty of up to 500% ad valorem on goods from Russia; the order describes the duty as applying to Russian goods subject to statutory exceptions and waivers, rather than specifically stating that all Russian energy products are included.
It also permits a 100% additional duty on goods from the five largest purchasers of Russian crude oil or natural gas, and a further 100% duty on goods from the five largest facilitators of Russian oil-sanctions evasion. The October 16 order activates these measures but immediately suspends their application.
The suspension remains in force until the President or the Secretary of State, in consultation with other administration officials, determines that the measures should be applied.
The immediate reason for the waiver appears to be economic and political rather than a change in Washington’s position on Russia.
The waiver avoids making those purchases commercially impossible through a 500% tariff.
Latin American Exposure to Russian Diesel and Fertiliser
Latin America is not identified in the available reporting as part of the act’s initial five largest Russian-energy buyers. The exact designation depends on the statutory methodology and subsequent US determinations.
That does not make Latin American countries immune. The law targets qualifying Russian energy purchases and gives the administration monitoring authority over countries that buy Russian-origin crude or gas or help evade sanctions.
The most exposed Latin American market is Brazil, a major agricultural economy and a major importer of fertiliser, including Russian fertiliser.
A key analytical distinction is necessary: Russian fertiliser is not identical to Russian crude oil or natural gas under the reported wording of the secondary-tariff provisions.
The act’s reported 100% measure is aimed principally at countries purchasing Russian crude oil or gas.
The Brazil Trade Angle
Brazil is especially important because its Russian relationship is concentrated in fertilisers, not merely energy.
Disruptions would affect Brazilian farmers, input distributors, crop margins and ultimately food prices. For Brazil, the immediate impact of the waiver is therefore an improvement in supply certainty.
Brazilian importers can continue negotiating Russian fertiliser cargoes without an immediate US secondary tariff. Banks, insurers and shipping companies receive temporary relief from the risk that a Brazilian customer could suddenly become subject to punitive US measures.
Brazilian farmers could face higher fertiliser costs because Brazil imports substantial volumes of fertiliser, including from Russia. Brazil retains flexibility to buy Russian energy or fertiliser while maintaining its broader foreign-policy position of strategic autonomy.
The commercial benefit is conditional. A US tariff on Brazilian exports would not be imposed simply because Brazil imports Russian fertiliser unless Brazil falls within the act’s covered categories or Washington applies a broader interpretation. The principal current threat is therefore uncertainty, not an already applicable Brazilian penalty.
What the Waiver Means for US Firms
For US companies, the waiver is a short-term commercial relief measure with a long-term compliance cost. Energy companies and fuel buyers benefit because Russian diesel can enter US supply chains without the threatened 500% duty.
However, they still face reputational, sanctions-screening and payment risks, particularly if the transaction involves entities covered by earlier Russia sanctions. Importers and manufacturers avoid an immediate price shock.
A tariff of up to 500% on Russian goods, including Russian energy products, could have affected Russian-origin imports into the United States, while a 100% tariff on goods from major Russian-energy buyers could have raised costs across unrelated supply chains. Banks, insurers and logistics companies must continue monitoring counterparties and cargo origins.
The waiver does not erase earlier sanctions, and the order directs US agencies to monitor Russian-energy purchases and sanctions evasion. US exporters remain exposed to retaliation if the administration later activates the duties.
The prospect of retaliation is itself a reason for companies to avoid treating the waiver as permanent.
If the Waiver Ends
If President Trump or the Secretary of State terminates the waiver, the consequences would likely include higher landed costs. A 500% US duty on Russian goods would have sharply increased the cost of direct Russian imports.
A 100% duty on goods from covered buyer countries would similarly penalise exports from those countries, not only the Russian-energy transaction itself. Trade diversion and supply disruption would follow.
Russian diesel and fertiliser would be redirected toward markets outside the US tariff perimeter. Latin American buyers might gain access to discounted cargoes, but competition for shipping, insurance and payment channels would intensify.
Brazilian agricultural inflation could result if fertiliser trade became subject to broader sanctions or if banks and insurers withdrew from Russian-linked transactions. Brazilian import costs could rise even without a direct tariff on Brazil.
Retaliation against US companies is a further risk.
Coercion Without Commitment
The waiver is best understood as coercion without commitment. Washington has preserved the threat needed to pressure Russia, energy buyers and sanctions facilitators, but it has avoided imposing costs that would immediately raise US fuel prices or disrupt relations with China, India, Turkey and other major purchasers.
For Brazil and other Latin American importers, the message is clear: Russian fertiliser and energy remain commercially available, but their political risk has increased. The waiver lowers today’s risk premium; it does not remove tomorrow’s tariff risk.
For US firms, the prudent assumption is that the waiver is revocable leverage, not a durable exemption. Companies should continue screening Russian-origin cargoes, reviewing country-of-origin rules, mapping indirect exposure through Latin American and Asian suppliers, and modelling a scenario in which the 100% and 500% duties take effect with little notice.
The legal structure creates a meaningful distinction between formal exposure and current enforcement. Importers and trading partners are not paying the new duties today, but they must operate under a framework in which the tariff threat remains legally available and can be reactivated by executive decision.
What It Means for You
If you import goods into the United States, the russia sanctions waiver means you are not paying the new duties today, but you should not assume they will never apply. The order leaves the tariff framework in place and preserves the administration’s ability to reverse course.
If you export from the United States to China, India, Turkey or other major Russian-energy buyers, you should model the risk of retaliatory tariffs if the waiver ends. The prospect of countermeasures is itself a reason to diversify markets and review contract clauses.
If you bank, insure or ship goods involving Russian-origin cargoes or Latin American counterparties, your compliance obligations have not disappeared. The waiver does not erase earlier sanctions, and the order directs US agencies to monitor Russian-energy purchases and sanctions evasion.
What Is Not Known
Available sources identify China, India, and Turkey as major buyers of Russian energy, but do not establish a complete, verified ranking showing that no Latin American country is among the five largest buyers, and they provide no official Latin America-specific buyer list or trade values. Exact country-by-country 2026 import values should be verified against Brazil’s Comex Stat, Mexico’s INEGI and SAT data, Argentina’s INDEC data, and UN Comtrade before publication.
The waiver has no fixed expiration date, and no scheduled six-month expiration date is reported for the Graham Act waiver itself. Its continuation depends on a later determination by President Trump or designated administration officials, rather than on a fixed date.
It is not clear whether the administration will apply a broader interpretation of the act to cover Russian fertiliser purchases, which are not identical to crude oil or natural gas under the reported wording of the secondary-tariff provisions. The exact designation of the five largest buyers also depends on the statutory methodology and subsequent US determinations.
What to Watch
Watch for any statement from President Trump or Secretary of State Marco Rubio indicating that the waiver will be terminated or modified. The order allows either official, in consultation with other administration officials, to determine when further action is appropriate.
Monitor the November 2026 midterm elections. The waiver followed a temporary easing of sanctions on Russian diesel exports intended to ease a supply crunch and lower fuel prices, and the political calculus could shift after election day.
Track the separate temporary easing of sanctions on Russian diesel exports, which runs until 7 April 2027 under OFAC General License 135.
Watch for any US designation of Brazil, Mexico or Argentina as a major purchaser, a sanctions-evasion facilitator or a country assisting Russian trade. Such a designation would turn an input-sourcing decision into a bilateral trade problem.
Finally, monitor Brazilian fertiliser import data from Comex Stat and Russian petroleum-product trade flows through UN Comtrade. Any significant increase in Russian-origin purchases could attract Washington’s attention and raise the risk of a future designation.

THE DAILY BS: HOW MUCH CAN YOU HANDLE?
SPARE ME THE BS (I’ve got things to do).
- Trump signed an executive order Friday waiving major sanctions and tariffs under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act.
- The paused measures included a 500% tariff on Russian goods and 100% duties targeting major purchasers of Russian oil and gas.
- The White House cited U.S. national interests; previously existing Russia sanctions remain in place, and the new measures could be reinstated.
LAY IT ON ME (I’ve got time).
President Donald Trump just put one of Washington’s biggest anti-Russia sanctions packages on ice.
And the timing is hard to miss.
With new penalties scheduled to take effect Sunday, Trump signed an executive order Friday waiving major portions of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026.
The legislation, which Trump himself signed September 18, included some eye-popping economic weapons.
A 500 percent tariff on Russian imports. Another 100 percent tariff targeting the largest importers of Russian oil and natural gas. Additional penalties aimed at countries facilitating sanctions evasion.
Then, two days before the measures were scheduled to take effect, the president reached for the waiver authority Congress had included in the law.
Trump’s explanation appears in the executive order itself.
“I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver at this time is in the national interests of the United States.”
That’s the administration’s official justification.
And it comes at a particularly consequential moment for energy markets.
Trump has been seeking ways to ease fuel prices amid disruptions associated with the conflict involving Iran. His administration has also pursued arrangements allowing additional Russian petroleum supplies to reach international markets.
Higher sanctions on countries purchasing Russian energy could complicate that strategy.
But they were precisely the kind of pressure Sen. Lindsey Graham and other supporters of the legislation wanted to impose on Moscow.
The law was designed to raise the economic cost of Russia’s war against Ukraine while pressuring foreign governments that continue buying Russian oil and gas.
Trump’s order does not repeal the law.
It suspends the application of major provisions using a presidential waiver explicitly authorized by Congress.
The order states that the exemptions will remain in effect “until such time as the President or the Secretary of State” determines that further action is appropriate, following required consultations.
That leaves the administration free to reconsider the sanctions later.
Another distinction matters: This is not a blanket elimination of every sanction Washington has imposed on Russia.
The executive order expressly preserves existing measures imposed under an earlier Russia-related national emergency.
So reports that Trump has simply ended all Russian sanctions would be inaccurate.
Still, the scale of the waived penalties is substantial.
A 500 percent import tariff is not the sort of economic threat Moscow or its trading partners could easily ignore.
Likewise, the potential 100 percent duties on major energy purchasers were intended to make continued Russian oil purchases considerably more expensive.
Instead, those new duties are being held back.
The move also puts Trump’s increasingly strained relationship with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky into sharper focus.
Trump has criticized Ukraine’s strikes against Russian oil infrastructure, arguing that the attacks contribute to higher international fuel prices.
Zelensky maintains that Russian energy revenues help finance Moscow’s invasion and that Ukraine has legitimate reasons to target infrastructure supporting the war.
Ukraine’s position is straightforward: Reducing the pressure on Russia risks giving Vladimir Putin additional resources and breathing room.
Trump’s calculation appears to be different.
He is prioritizing the immediate consequences for American energy costs while reserving the option to restore new sanctions if circumstances change.
For supporters of economic pressure on Moscow, Friday’s decision raises questions about whether a bipartisan sanctions law will ever be fully enforced.
For the White House, the waiver preserves flexibility during volatile energy markets and diplomatic negotiations.
DBS WIRE SOURCES (I’ve got all day).
