- CBS News — Trump waives Russian oil tariffs before law takes effect
- Financial Times — Trump exempts Russia from additional sanctions

sources.news_title: Starlink restrictions in Ukraine a ‘planned operation’, Zelenskyy says
sources.text:
Starlink restrictions hampering Ukraine’s war effort are “a planned operation,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Saturday.
The satellite service operated by Elon Musk’s SpaceX is still deactivated in Ukraine at speeds over 160 km/h, which prevents some of its drones to intercept high-speed Shahed drones used by Russia, Zelenskyy told reporters in a WhatsApp chat.
He added that Ukraine conducted a test by sending Starlink-equipped vehicules to European Union countries, at speeds over 180 km/h. “Starlink kept working … The conclusion is this: the restrictions are in effect in Ukraine, but they are not in effect in European Union countries. So, this is a planned operation,” Zelenskyy said.
Advertisement
The restrictions have revived questions on Ukraine’s reliance on the satellite system operated by a U.S. company amid escalating tensions between Kyiv and the White House. “This will cost many of us our lives,” an experienced Ukrainian officer told POLITICO and the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network earlier this week.
“We’re reaching out to everyone at the military level, at the Ministry of Defense level, and at the diplomatic level, including to SpaceX. Right now, no one is responding to our military or the Ministry of Defense,” Zelenskyy told reporters.
The European Union is under increasing pressure to provide Ukraine with an alternative to Starlink. But negotiations between Brussels and Kyiv over access to the bloc’s Govsatcom program — which gives participating governments secure communications capabilities— have been stalling. And IRIS², the EU’s in-house planned network to match Starlink, is only expected to come online in 2030.
“The Europeans are now raising the question of alternatives themselves. And they’re already working on them. They’re already making progress, and they’ll succeed in this area. I can already see that,” Zelenskyy said.
SpaceX did not immediately responded to a request for comment.
Earlier on Saturday, Zelenskyy accused Russia of looking to create a blackout across Ukraine, amid attacks on energy infrastructure and the waiver of U.S. sanctions on Moscow.
Advertisement
“Russia is trying to cause a blackout in Ukraine right before winter. Russia is trying to leave millions of our people without electricity and heating. Pressure is needed to stop this,” he said on Telegram.
“An American sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, monetary rewards for [Russian President Vladimir] Putin: all of this only encourages him to keep striking,” he added.
The Ukrainian leader’s comments come after Russia carried out strikes on the war-torn country’s energy sector, including power generation and transmission facilities, with more than 320 jet-powered Shahed drones, loitering munitions, cruise and ballistic missiles. Power was reportedly cut for about 1 million people.
They also come as U.S. President Donald Trump signed on Friday an executive order that waived key sanctions on Russia — a decision that Kirill Dmitriev, Putin’s special envoy for investment and economic cooperation, described as “an important and truly historic moment.” Trump’s move comes only a few days after he made a deal with Putin over supplying barrels of diesel, leaving European countries and Ukraine stunned.
“A decision was unfortunately made in America to completely ignore Lindsey Graham’s bill, which was supposed to introduce truly effective pressure on Russia to end this war,” Zelenskyy said. “This bill could have helped a great deal, and it still can! But the law needs to actually work, and every vote for it matters.”
This article was updated. Veronika Melkozerova contributed reporting.

sources.news_title: Trump waives Russia's "hellish" sanctions two days before they bite
sources.text:
US President Donald Trump has put a sweeping package of sanctions and tariffs under the Graham Act on hold and given Russia a comprehensive waiver only two days before it was due to take effect, AP reported on October 17.
Trump signed an executive order on October 16 telling Congress that the pause was in the US national interest. He had signed the so-called “sanctions from hell” – or more formally, the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act - into law only on September 18, and its sanctions and tariffs had to be imposed by October 18 unless he waived them.
The package was sponsored by the late Senator Lindsey Graham, a long-time ally of Ukraine, who proposed imposing 500% tariffs on third countries that continue to do business with Russia – specifically they targeted India and China that continue to fund the Kremlin budget by buying large amounts of oil. The package was designed to give the Trump administration powerful tools to break the back of the Russian economy and force Russian President Vladimir Putin to the negotiating table to end the Ukraine conflict.
Trump has done the opposite. The White House did not explain how the waiver served the national interest; it said a report setting out its reasons had been sent to Congress.
The waiver guts the toughest US sanctions bill of the war only a month after Trump signed it, and it comes days after his diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin lifted sanctions on Russian fuel to bring down US pump prices. Washington is easing the pressure on Moscow just as Russia steps up its winter campaign to freeze Ukraine into submission when Kyiv needs help the most. As IntelliNews reported, the heating season has just kicked off in Ukraine just as Russian drones and missiles plunged its biggest cities into darkness.
The law, championed by Graham, who died in mandated blocking sanctions on top Russian entities including Sberbank, VTB, Gazprombank and the Russian central bank, with secondary sanctions on foreign banks that deal with them, allowed shadow fleet tankers to be blocked directly, and authorised tariffs of up to 500% on Russian goods and up to 100% on the five biggest buyers of Russian oil and gas, according to a summary by law firm Covington. Section 115 lets the president waive any of it with a report certifying the waiver is “in the national interest,” with no time limit.
The executive order formally sets the 500% duty on Russian goods and the 100% duty on the top five importers, then largely waives both, the Kyiv Independent reported. The tariffs now sit on the books, switched off, for Trump to use whenever he chooses.
"These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, and everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin," said Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal, who co-wrote the law with Graham. Democratic Representative Don Beyer said Trump had waived "all of the sanctions on Russia" in the act, "just as I and others warned he would". A bipartisan group of senators had asked Trump on October 13 to scrap the diesel deal and enforce the law instead.
The waiver comes at a time when Trump appears to have broken with Ukraine completely after his conversation with Putin. He has also cancelled the Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) programme where Europe can buy US weapons on Ukraine’s behalf, threatened to stop sharing satellite intelligence and throttled Ukraine’s access to the Starlink communications system that in effect makes Ukraine’s drones inoperable.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy warned on October 16 that the diesel deal would open the door to more relief. "In my view, we cannot accept these agreements. Because gas deals will follow. And I am absolutely certain of this. After gas, they will lift sanctions on other things as well," he said, according to the Kyiv Independent.
And indeed, Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and Putin's investment envoy Kirill Dmitriev discussed the possibility of bringing in a US investor to restart Russia’s gas deliveries to Europe in October. Dmitriev has said in recent days that a large package of business deals is still being discussed with the Trump administration as part of a round of meetings in the last week.
More relief in the pipeline
Washington is also weighing easing sanctions on shadow fleet tankers to bring down freight rates, and Trump earlier backed a plan to trade sanctions relief for prisoners.
Dmitriev said on October 16 that Moscow and Washington were discussing joint projects including nuclear-powered data centres. "Naturally, progress is quite difficult; there is resistance - widespread resistance, in fact, from various quarters. Yet, as the diesel example demonstrates, I believe we will soon announce several other significant initiatives. The ice has, in fact, begun to break," Dmitriev said, Reuters reported.
The two presidents are getting on well. Their call on October 9, when the diesel deal was agreed, lasted an hour and a half and "nobody wanted to hang up first", Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said, TASS reported.
Almost no new sanctions
The about face on the hellish sanctions and the obvious bonhomie of last week’s telephone call only underscore Trump’s continued affiliation with Putin and his preference for doing business with Russia over rescuing Ukraine in its hour of need.
Trump has imposed almost new sanctions on Russia since returning to the White House and indeed, exempted it entirely from his Liberation Day tariffs on most of the rest of the world.
The one significant move was the blacklisting of oil majors Rosneft and Lukoil in October 2025, but analysts said at the time that Russia's buyers, mainly India and China, would soon find workarounds, and Russian oil continued to flow through other sellers and the shadow fleet.
In 2025, Trump's first year back in office, the US added 74 Russian persons to its main sanctions list, the Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) list, and no Russian entities to the Commerce Department's Entity List, according to the Center for a New American Security (CNAS). Under President Joe Biden the US added 1,706 Russian persons to the SDN list in 2024 alone.
| Year | Administration | Russian persons added to SDN list | Russian persons added to Entity List | 
| 2022 | Biden | not published by CNAS | 374 | 
| 2023 | Biden | 1,227 (persons located in Russia) | 207 | 
| 2024 | Biden | 1,706 | 147 | 
| 2025 | Trump | 74 | 0 | 
US Russia sanctions designations by year. Source: CNAS, Sanctions by the Numbers, 2023, 2024 and 2025 year in review. The 2023 SDN figure counts sanctioned persons located in Russia; CNAS puts all Russia-related SDN designations that year at 1,522.
Kyiv's relations with the White House are at their lowest since the Oval Office row of February 2025. Trump's envoys threatened to cut off intelligence sharing, including warnings of missile launches, unless Ukraine stopped hitting Russian refineries, and the US pressed Kyiv on intelligence as the energy truce collapsed. Zelenskiy said Ukraine received no advance warning of the Russian missiles that killed six people in Kyiv on October 13-14. An order to limit Ukraine's military access to Starlink also came from inside the White House, Reuters reported.
Add the sanctions waiver and those moves look less like neutrality than an effort to force an end to the war on Moscow's terms before the November 3 midterm elections. Zelenskiy has called the diesel deal a “betrayal” and said Kyiv is "losing" Washington as an ally. Trump countered by calling for Zelenskiy’s removal as president and followed up by calling him a “dictator” in a tweet.
The row has also soured US-EU relations, which is being forced into progressively more extreme positions to support its ally Ukraine. At the EU summit in Brussels on October 16 even Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis, long a Trump admirer, said: "Trump effectively betrayed us by concluding the business deal with Putin.”

sources.news_title: Trump Waives Sweeping Russia Sanctions — GOP Senators Erupt
sources.text:
President Donald Trump has used a national-interest waiver to pause the sweeping Russia sanctions Congress passed with overwhelming bipartisan support — and some of the sharpest criticism is coming from inside his own party.
The move does not repeal the new law. It does something more immediate: it suspends the law’s major economic penalties while the White House decides what comes next.
That distinction matters. So does the timing.
The order arrived just two days before the sanctions were due to take effect, as Russia continued pounding Ukraine’s energy system and the administration pursued a separate diplomatic and commercial track with Moscow.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia had just carried out one of its largest attacks on Ukraine’s energy sector, hitting more than 15 critical power-generation and transmission facilities across multiple regions. Repair crews were still working as the sanctions debate broke open in Washington.
Yesterday, the Russians carried out one of their largest attacks on Ukraine’s energy sector – more than 15 critical power generation and transmission facilities were targeted across different regions of Ukraine. Restoration work is ongoing, with all necessary services and all… pic.twitter.com/nEhkkjxwXa
— Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) October 17, 2026
The contrast is stark: the administration is withholding new economic pressure at the same moment Kyiv says Moscow is escalating attacks on the civilian power grid. That makes the waiver a test of whether promised leverage can alter Russian behavior before the penalties ever bite.
The legal mechanism is laid out in the administration’s own order, and it is broader than a routine enforcement delay. The decision reaches the central penalties Congress designed to squeeze both Moscow and the foreign buyers keeping its energy trade alive.
The White House executive order begins by implementing the new Russia and Iran sanctions law, which President Trump signed on September 18. It establishes a 500 percent duty on Russian goods and a 100 percent duty on goods from countries found to be buying or facilitating Russian oil and uranium.
The order also targets Russian officials, financial institutions, energy entities and vessels operating in Moscow’s so-called shadow fleet. Section 4 then invokes the statute’s national-interest authority and waives those duties, sanctions and restrictions until the president and senior officials determine that further action is warranted.
In plain English: the enforcement machinery is now built, but the president has pulled the emergency brake before it starts moving.
That gives Trump leverage. The administration can argue that it now holds a congressionally authorized economic hammer over Russia, China, India and any other country facilitating Moscow’s energy trade — without swinging it immediately.
It also gives critics an obvious counterargument: a hammer that never falls may not be leverage at all.
Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina did not bother with diplomatic language. He called the decision “beyond irresponsible” and stressed that the sanctions law passed the Senate 86-11.
Beyond irresponsible. What part of enforcing a law passed 86-11 by the Senate does the President and his advisors not understand? It’s unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine and butchers innocent civilians every…
— Senator Thom Tillis (@SenThomTillis) October 17, 2026
The dispute is especially combustible because the law bears the name of the late Senator Lindsey Graham, one of Trump’s closest allies and one of Washington’s most persistent advocates for crushing economic pressure on Moscow.
Senator John Cornyn of Texas made that point with one devastating line: “Lindsey would be appalled.”
Lindsey would be appalled: Trump Signs Order Exempting Russia From Sanctions Law https://t.co/9tF3CBc3pL
— Senator John Cornyn (@JohnCornyn) October 17, 2026
The Associated Press reports that the waiver landed shortly before the law’s implementation deadline, after Congress assembled a broad package aimed at Russian officials, banks, oil revenue and the fleet used to evade existing restrictions. The timing transformed what could have been a quiet administrative choice into an immediate confrontation with lawmakers who expected the penalties to take effect.
The report also points to a separate commercial agreement under which a U.S. company would provide diesel fuel to Russia. That deal helps explain why senators regard the waiver as a substantive policy turn instead of a technical pause.
Administration defenders describe the delay as part of a larger attempt to preserve negotiating room with Moscow. Critics see economic relief being offered before Russia has made a meaningful concession on Ukraine, attacks on civilian infrastructure or any durable peace framework.
The disagreement therefore concerns more than the calendar. It asks whether holding sanctions in reserve increases American leverage or signals that the White House is reluctant to use the authority Congress supplied.
Axios adds that the backlash extends beyond Democrats, with Republican senators who backed the bill publicly challenging the White House. Kyiv, meanwhile, is warning that Russian attacks remain relentless while the new economic penalties sit idle.
The secondary sanctions were designed to pressure Moscow through the countries and companies that sustain its energy trade. Major buyers and intermediaries would have to decide whether access to Russian oil and uranium justified exposure to punishing U.S. tariffs.
Waiving those penalties removes the immediate deadline that was supposed to force that choice. It also gives foreign governments and markets time to test whether the threat is likely to become policy.
There is a strategic case for Trump’s approach.
Presidents traditionally want flexibility in foreign policy. The threat of sanctions can sometimes extract more than sanctions themselves, particularly if the target believes relief can be exchanged for a concrete concession.
Trump has always preferred direct negotiation, maximum uncertainty and deal-making over a timetable set by Congress.
The order also preserves the legal architecture. If negotiations fail, the administration can move quickly without returning to Congress for another vote.
But there is a serious risk in that strategy.
Russia has watched Western governments announce red lines, negotiate over deadlines and dilute enforcement for years. Every delay teaches the Kremlin something about American resolve.
If Moscow concludes that the sanctions will always be postponed in the name of keeping talks alive, the threat becomes theater.
Congress wrote the waiver into the law, so Trump is exercising authority lawmakers themselves provided. That legal point is clear.
The political question is harder: why pass a sanctions package by overwhelming margins, name it for one of the Senate’s loudest Russia hawks, and then suspend its central penalties before they ever take effect?
The White House now owns the answer.
If the pause produces measurable Russian concessions — a ceasefire, reduced attacks, prisoner releases, verifiable limits or a durable peace framework — Trump will argue that flexibility succeeded where reflexive punishment would have failed.
If Russia takes the relief, continues its offensive and offers nothing substantial in return, the senators warning about capitulation will look prescient.
The fight reaches far beyond another Washington argument over procedure. It is a live test of whether Trump’s deal-making style can restrain Vladimir Putin when a massive congressional sanctions weapon is already loaded and ready.
For now, the weapon remains on the table.
President Trump is the one who decided not to fire it.

sources.news_title: Trump's decision to waive Russian sanctions outrages Congress
sources.text:
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump's abrupt decision to waive sanctions on Russia days before they were to take effect drew outrage Saturday from members of Congress, which had overwhelmingly passed the legislation in a bipartisan display of American support for Ukraine in the war with Russia.
Lawmakers from both parties blasted the executive order late Friday, the latest in a series of steps that the Republican president has taken drawing the United States closer to Russia's Vladimir Putin. Trump recently announced a diesel deal with Putin to import Russian energy in a long-shot effort to curb high gas prices in the U.S. that are roiling the midterm elections on Nov. 3.
“Beyond irresponsible,” said Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., on social media, hours after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy expressed hope that the sanctions that were supposed to take effect Sunday targeting Russian's economy could be revived.
“What part of enforcing a law passed 86-11 by the Senate does the President and his advisors not understand?” Tillis said. “It’s unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine.”
Tillis said that if Trump wants to actually bring down energy prices, he should resolve the Iran war, which is largely blamed for the spike at the pump, and “not by doing a solid for Vladimir Putin.”
Republican Sen. John Cornyn of Texas said “Lindsey would be appalled,” referring to the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., who worked endlessly on the bill before he died this summer. The bill is known as the Lindsey Graham Russian Sanctions Act.
Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer of New York said in a statement that “by giving the Russian economy life support, Trump’s deal with the devil keeps getting dirtier.”
Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., said Trump is “thumbing his nose” at Congress and “enabling Vladimir Putin to continue his war of aggression.” She urged her colleagues to take action to reverse course.
Trump's actions come as Ukraine is bracing for a stark winter confronting Russia's ongoing attacks on its energy infrastructure to heat homes and keep the lights on. Zelenskyy, who has endured a rocky relationship with Trump but stayed close to the U.S. lawmakers, urged supporters to speak out on behalf of the sanctions.
The next steps are highly uncertain with the House and Senate are on recess until after Election Day. Trump said he was waiving the sanctions indefinitely, citing national security concerns. It is unlikely Congress would be in a position to take any action to challenge Trump’s moves until lawmakers return to Washington.
Skeptics in Congress warned Trump would not follow the law
It took almost a year for Graham to persuade Trump to agree to the Russian sanctions package. It was designed to impose steep tariffs on countries that import large amounts of Russian oil and energy products and was promoted as way to halt the flow of funds fueling Putin's four-year war against Ukraine.
But even as Zelenskyy had watched from the visitor gallery as the Senate advanced the package after Graham's death, skeptics in Congress warned Trump would be unlikely to follow the bill once he had signed it into law a month ago.
Last week, a bipartisan group of senators urged the Trump administration to more quickly clamp down on Russia, particularly the “shadow fleet” of tankers that Moscow is using to transport oil and bypass America’s sanctions. The senators noted that the bulk of the new law's provisions were to be effective Sunday.
Instead, Trump soon announced the diesel deal with Putin, saying that Russia had agreed to supply tons of fuel to the U.S., where gas prices have skyrocketed in some areas and voters saying affordability issues are a top concern.
Outraged lawmakers have pledged to stop the Trump-Putin deal.
New York Rep. Gregory Meeks, the ranking Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee who had led opposition to the Graham bill — warning that Trump would flout the law — introduced legislation Friday that would block Trump's diesel deal with Putin. “At a time when the United States should be increasing pressure on the Kremlin, Donald Trump is cozying up to Putin and striking self-enriching deals instead of standing with Ukraine," Meeks said in a statement.
He called the deal “corrupt” and said it “goes against everything the United States stands for.”
On Saturday, he said that "Congress is not helpless" and must act.
Graham's legacy on the line
Graham's sister, Darline Graham of South Carolina, helped ensure Senate passage of the bill, once she was appointed by the state's governor to fill her brother's seat.
She is now running against Democrat Annie Andrews in a tight race. Trump is expected in the state next week to rally voters.
“Look, the president and I share the same goal, which is to end the war, to get gas and diesel prices down, and the sanctions bill is one of the tools he can use to do that,” Darline Graham said at a campaign stop Saturday.
“It’s up to him whether or not he chooses to use it. Personally, I would choose to keep the pressure on Russia,” she said, “because I don’t trust Putin and I don’t trust Russia.”
Like her brother, who often publicly parted ways with the president, Darline Graham said she and Trump can have their differences.
“I am proud of it to help get across the finish line. It meant a lot to Lindsey,” she said. “But you know, like Lindsey, he disagreed with the president sometimes they had that relationship where they could agree to disagree sometimes. And I think that just happens."
__
Associated Press writers Meg Kinnard in Mount Pleasant, S.C., and Kevin Freking and Mary Clare Jalonick contributed to this report.

sources.news_title: Trump signs order exempting Russia from sanctions legislation
sources.text:
Trump signs order exempting Russia from sanctions legislation
Published 12:05 am Saturday, October 17, 2026
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump signed an executive order Friday night exempting Russia from a new sanctions measure that Congress passed last month, offering another economic lifeline to Russian President Vladimir Putin as the United States turns to Russia for help in lowering gas prices.
The sanctions were intended to target Russian officials, oligarchs and financial institutions, and were part of a law that was named after Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., who died in July after spending more than a year building support for the measure. The law, which is designed to squeeze the financial lifelines sustaining Russia’s war against Ukraine, also provided Trump with additional tariff authority that he could use to punish countries that continue to trade with Russia.
The White House has broad authority to issue sanctions exemptions or waivers, and the new law requires Trump to notify Congress only if he opts against imposing the economic restrictions on Russia. Two days before the law was set to take effect, Trump exercised that power.
“I am hereby waiving the application of such sanctions, restrictions and duties provided for in the Graham Act,” Trump said in the order. “I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver at this time is in the national interests of the United States.”
The order does not explain why waiving the sanctions is in the interests of the United States or what rationale Trump is providing to Congress for the waivers.
The decision comes as Trump has in recent weeks embraced Russia and turned against Ukraine amid frustration that Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries are pushing up oil prices around the world. Elevated oil prices are making gasoline more expensive in the United States, fueling inflation weeks ahead of midterm elections that could cost Republicans control of Congress.
Trump announced last week that he had reached a deal with Putin, and that the United States would begin importing Russian diesel fuel. The Treasury Department temporarily lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports “to allow the supply of Russian diesel to the global market,” and gave Russian energy producers a general license to sell diesel fuel until April.
That decision angered President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of Ukraine, and drew backlash from European officials. This week, a bipartisan group of senators urged Trump to reverse the sanctions waiver on diesel fuel.
The move to waive the sanctions that were enacted in the new law drew a swift rebuke from critics in Congress, who had predicted that Trump would not impose them.
“Trump’s latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression,” said Rep. Don Beyer, D-Va.
Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., the ranking member on the Banking Committee, called Trump’s move an “abject failure” of leadership.
“By waiving these sanctions, Trump is thumbing his nose at Congress’ direction that he ratchet up pressure on the Kremlin, and enabling Vladimir Putin to continue his war of aggression,” Warren said.
The sanctions law was the brainchild of Graham, a Russia hawk and close ally of Trump’s. The legislation, which was set to take effect on Oct. 18, won bipartisan support despite concern that the president would not heed the sanctions requirements, and that he would potentially misuse the tariff authority.
The law gave Trump the power to target countries importing Russian oil and gas with up to 100% tariffs, subject all Russian imports to the United States to up to 500% tariffs, and take greater aim at Russia’s “shadow fleet” of oil tankers and banking system.
In the executive order, Trump said that the United States would “monitor” the purchases of Russian oil by other countries and that his advisers would recommend whether to take further action on tariffs.
It is not clear if waiving some of the sanctions means that Russia will be welcomed back into the Western financial system after years of being an outcast.
“The underlying sanctions architecture remains in place, and no one wants to be caught holding the risk when the waiver is pulled,” said Daniel Tannebaum, a partner at Oliver Wyman, a consulting firm that advises banks on anti-money laundering and sanctions matters. “I’m not sure what positive impact to the American economy will be derived in reality.”

sources.news_title: Trump Waives Key Russia-Related Sanctions and Tariffs Before New Law Takes Effect
sources.text:
President Donald Trump waived key sanctions and tariffs related to Russia just days before they were set to take effect under a law he signed last month. This included duties on Russian goods and penalties for purchasing Russian oil and gas. Trump stated that the waiver is in the national interest of the United States.
The law was designed to put pressure on Russia for its invasion of Ukraine that started in 2022. However, Trump has been showing support for Moscow while criticizing Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy. The timing of this waiver is significant, as it comes just before the US midterm elections, where Trump’s party is trying to retain control of Congress. Analysts noted that implementing the new measures could have increased oil prices amid rising costs linked to the US-Israeli conflict with Iran.
The legislation, backed primarily by the late Senator Lindsey Graham, aimed to impose tariffs up to 100% on goods imported from the top five importers of Russian oil and gas. The waiver will remain until Trump or his officials decide further action is needed. Countries like China and India have expressed concerns regarding the sanctions.
US Representative Don Beyer criticized Trump, claiming the waiver undermines US efforts against Russia and betrays Ukraine. Trump has also faced backlash from some lawmakers over a recent diesel deal with Russia, which they believe would support Russia’s war efforts. Putin’s envoy hailed Trump’s waiver as a significant moment that could have halted US-Russia economic cooperation.
With information from Reuters

Rusia încearcă să-i lase pe milioane dintre compatrioţii noştri fără curent şi încălzire", a postat preşedintele ucrainean pe reţelele sociale, făcând apel la aliaţi "să facă presiune" asupra Moscovei pentru ca acest lucru să înceteze.
Rusia a atacat peste 15 facilităţi energetice în regiuni centrale şi vestice în cursul nopţii, a acuzat Zelenski.
"Rusia şi-a extins campania împotriva sistemului energetic şi încearcă să afecteze cât mai mult rezervele Ucrainei şi capacitatea de a efectua reparaţii", a menţionat pe Telegram şeful statului ucrainean, potrivit Reuters.
Ministerul rus al Apărării a anunţat sâmbătă că a comis un atac la scară largă în timpul nopţii asupra unor ţinte din infrastructura Ucraineană, inclusiv asupra celei mai mari oţelării a ţării, din oraşul Krivoi Rog, relatează Reuters, citată de Agerpres.
Fabrica este în proprietatea gigantului oţelului ArcelorMittal, care a suspendat activitatea în septembrie după o serie de lovituri ruseşti cu rachete balistice.
Într-un comunicat, ministerul a precizat că oţelăria aproviziona cu produse din oţel complexul militaro-industrial ucrainean.
Potrivit sursei citate, o substaţie de electricitate din oraşul Jitomir, din nordul Ucrainei, a fost de asemenea lovită, la fel ca şi o oţelărie din Zaporojie, oraş aflat în apropiere de linia frontului.
Un cargou din Marea Neagră a fost de asemenea lovit, a precizat Ministerul rus al Apărării, afirmând că acesta transporta încărcătură militară în portul ucrainean Odesa.
Reuters precizează că nu a putut confirma independent informaţiile făcute publice de ministerul rus.

sources.news_title: Trump enforces and “freezes” the Graham Act’s Russia sanctions and tariffs on the same day – “in the national interest”
sources.text:
US President Donald Trump signed an executive order on Friday, October 16, to implement the “Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026” and, in the same text, suspended almost all the measures it provides for. The order, posted late in the evening on the White House website, two days before the October 18 deadline, sets in its second section an additional 500% tariff on goods from Russia and 100% on goods from the five largest importers of Russian oil and natural gas, if they make new purchases, as well as from the five main facilitators of sanctions evasion.
In the fourth section, however, Trump invokes section 115 of the Act, which lets him suspend any measure if he certifies to Congress that it serves the national interest. “I am suspending the application of all tariffs provided for in sections 112 and 113 of the Graham Act or in this order,” he says, adding that he has submitted the certification and a related report to Congress. The sanctions of most of the Act’s articles, which target Russian officials, banks and the “shadow fleet” of tankers, are also suspended. The exemptions apply until the president or the secretary of state judge that new action is needed. Sanctions already in force under earlier orders are unaffected, and the US Trade Representative will monitor purchases of Russian energy and brief the president.
The Act, which Trump signed on September 18, is named after Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, who died suddenly in July after a trip to Ukraine. It was drafted by him and Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal and passed with large bipartisan majorities. The White House did not explain why the suspension serves the national interest. The decision comes a week after the deal on Russian diesel, which has already drawn reactions in Congress.
“Trump just suspended all the Russia sanctions in the Graham Act, as I and others had warned,” Democratic Representative Don Beyer wrote on X, calling on Congress to “fix this flawed law”. Volodymyr Zelensky had said the same day in Brussels that Ukraine cannot accept such deals, warning that “after gas, they will lift sanctions on other things”. Relations between Washington and Kyiv have worsened after Trump’s criticism of Ukrainian strikes on refineries, which he called a “disgrace”.

sources.news_title: Donald Trump waives Russia sanctions as row with Zelensky intensifies
sources.text:
Donald Trump has blocked numerous sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to take effect, as a row with his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky deepens.
The sanctions were passed by the US Congress and signed into law by Trump in September.
But the US president issued an executive order on Friday night saying that suspending some was in the US “national interest”, prompting a backlash from US lawmakers.
It comes after the White House said Katie Zacharia is “transitioning out” of the role of press secretary just days after taking the job.
The US president said on Friday he suggested to Zacharia she should “reconsider” the job.

sources.news_title: Trump Suspends Tariffs and Sanctions on Russia Set Out in Graham Act
sources.text:
US President Donald Trump has suspended the application of tariffs and sanctions provided for by Senator Lindsey Graham’s sanctions law targeting Russia and Iran, which he signed in September 2026. At the same time, the order formally establishes tariff restrictions but includes a provision waiving their application.
This is stated in the US president’s order.
The law provides for the introduction of 100% tariffs on goods from five countries that import the most Russian oil. The document also provided for 500% tariffs on goods from Russia and sanctions against a number of Russian entities.
The deadline for implementing the relevant provisions was 18 October 2026.
However, Trump made use of a provision in the law that allows the president to waive the application of the restrictions set out in it.
"I have submitted to Congress a certification that waiving their application at this stage is in the national interests of the United States," Trump said.
Section 115 of the Graham Act allows the president to waive the application of sanctions, restrictions and tariffs if he submits to Congress a written certification that such a decision is in the national interests of the United States. The president must also provide a report explaining the grounds for this decision.
At the same time, the order does not отменяет sanctions imposed earlier by other US executive orders against Russia. The specified exceptions will remain in effect until the US president or the secretary of state, following appropriate consultations, decide that further measures are required.
On 19 September, President Trump signed the bill on sanctions against Russia and Iran, authored by the late Senator Lindsey Graham.
- The administration of US President Donald Trump expects that an agreement to supply Russian diesel fuel will help bring Moscow back to talks on ending the war against Ukraine.
- On 9 October, Trump announced an agreement that would see millions of tonnes of Russian diesel fuel reach global markets. This could ease sanctions pressure on Moscow and increase its revenues from energy exports.
- On 12 October, the US president dismissed intelligence reports that Russia is passing information about US military facilities to Iran. And on Tuesday he again defended the deal on Russian diesel fuel, rejecting concerns that the proceeds could finance Russia’s war machine.
